readerTitle: A good number starts with a goal
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 화원, 상담팀, 점심 식당) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 숫자를 고르기 전에 목표와 그 숫자로 내릴 결정을 먼저 적는다. 같은 숫자도 목표에 따라 좋은 신호가 되기도 하고 나쁜 신호가 되기도 한다.
misconception: 재기 쉽고 많이 오르는 숫자를 지켜보면 사업이 잘되고 있는지 알 수 있다.

sources.text: 측정과 의사결정의 일반 원칙 (목표 → 결정 → 지표 순서로 지표를 정하는 방식)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 3번 카드 차트: 방문객 수 +20%, 전체 매출 +3%, 화분 판매 0%. 방문객이 늘고 매출이 거의 그대로인 상황은 객단가가 낮은 할인 상품 구매가 늘었다는 설정으로 설명됩니다.
실제 기업·연구 사례나 통계는 쓰지 않았습니다. 같은 단위의 THK-06-05(굿하트의 법칙)와 겹치지 않도록, 지표가 목표가 되면 왜곡된다는 내용은 7번 카드에서 한 문장으로만 언급했습니다.

cards.title: A good number starts with a goal
body: Maya runs a garden centre. Last month she put a small counter above the door, and every evening she checks it before locking up.
This month the count is up 20%. She feels great. Then she looks at the shelf at the back, and the planters she cared most about are still sitting there.

image.label: A door counter showing a rising number above a shop entrance
image.brief: 따뜻한 3D 일러스트. 작은 화원 입구 위에 디지털 방문객 카운터가 큰 숫자를 보여줌. 앞쪽 주인은 카운터를 보며 미소 짓고, 뒤편 선반에는 팔리지 않은 큰 화분들이 그대로 놓여 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Is the new window display working?
body: Maya built the display to sell more of her seasonal planters. They earn far more per sale than anything else, but they sit at the back where few people look.
Which number tells her whether the display is doing its job?

options.text: How many people walk through the door each day
options.feedback: Easy to count and it moves fast. But people can come in, browse the front and leave without ever reaching the planters.

options.text: Total weekly sales across the shop
options.feedback: It matters, but weather, holidays and every other product move it too. A real change in planters could hide inside the total.

options.text: How many seasonal planters sell each week
options.feedback: It moves when the display does what it was built to do, and stays flat when it doesn't. You lose the big-picture view, so keep total sales in sight as a check.

cards.title: The door said yes. The goal said no.
body: Maya had placed cheap sale items at the front of the display to catch the eye. It worked. More people came in, bought a $3 seed packet and left.
The number she watched every evening rose. The number tied to her goal didn't move at all.

image.label: The door said yes. The goal said no.

cards.title: Metrics start from goals
body: A **metric** is a number you track to judge how things are going. On its own, it means nothing. It only means something as an answer to a question.
So the order matters. First, the goal: what are we trying to achieve? Then the decision: what would we do differently depending on the answer? Only then, the number.
Maya started with the number that was easy to count. Her goal came second, so the counter answered a question she never asked.
cards.softwareNote: Sign-ups are the door counter of software. If the goal is paying customers, the number to watch is how many sign-ups become paying customers, not how many arrive.

cards.title: Three questions before you pick a number.
body: Before you put a number on the board, write down three answers:
list: **The goal:** what are we trying to make happen?
**The decision:** what will we do if the number goes up, and what if it goes down?
**The test:** does this number move when, and mostly when, we get closer to the goal?
cards.callout: If no answer to question two comes to mind, the number is decoration.

cards.title: Fast calls can be good news or bad news.
body: A support team tracks calls answered per hour. If the goal is to clear a backlog after a storm cut power to half the town, rising calls per hour is exactly right.
If the goal is to fix each problem on the first call, the same rise may mean people are being rushed off the phone and calling back tomorrow.
The number didn't change. The goal did, and with it what the number means.

cards.title: Some goals can't be counted directly.
body: "Make customers love us" has no counter. You'll need a stand-in, such as repeat visits or referrals. That's fine, as long as you remember it's a stand-in and check now and then that it still tracks the real goal.
Also, once people are judged on a number, they find ways to move it that skip the goal. And goals change. A metric picked last year may answer last year's question.

cards.title: Now it's a lunch restaurant.
body: Your restaurant sits among offices. Most guests have under an hour for lunch. Your goal: stop losing the guests who give up and leave when food takes too long. You've added a short express menu.
Which number shows whether it's working?

options.feedback: A cheaper express menu may lower it even while you win back guests. You'd read success as failure.
It should rise if the menu works, but rainy days and office holidays move it too. It's a useful backup, not the main signal.

options.text: Share of guests served within 10 minutes, plus how many walk out
options.feedback: Both move directly with the problem you set out to fix. They won't tell you about profit, so check that separately.

cards.title: Pick the goal first. Then the number.
body: A number is only as good as the question it answers. Start with the goal and the decision, and the right metric usually becomes obvious.
**Try it today:** take one number you check every week. Write the goal it serves and what you'd do if it doubled. If you can't, replace it.
